chunks.text: Wastewater is typically collected through sewage pipes in municipal areas. Treatment of wastewater entails a step-wise process that occurs in primary, secondary, and tertiary stages. Primary treatment involves basic screening and filtration processes to remove suspended solid waste and reduce its biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), which is an indicator to monitor water quality that assesses the amount of oxygen microorganisms must consume to break down the organic material present in wastewater (US EPA, 2012) . Primary treatment can reduce BOD by up to 30% (Flo ¨rke, 2013) . Secondary treatment uses biological processes to break down the dissolved organic matter remaining after primary treatment. Secondary treatment can remove up to 90% of BOD and total suspended solids (US EPA, 2004) . Any additional step in wastewater treatment is considered tertiary treatment (or ''advanced treatment''), which includes any purification process that continues beyond the previous steps and may require more complex technology such as ion exchange and reverse osmosis to further remove contaminants or phosphorous and nitrogen (World Bank, 2013b; US EPA, 2004) .

chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: Screens and grit removal are widely employed in WWTPs as they enhance the operation and maintenance of subsequent treatment units. Recent innovations in pretreatment technologies have brought the heavy cost of grit in WWTPs operations lower which has been considered an unavoidable burden. For example, based on advanced Grit Management™, Headcell® grit separation system was developed to achieve optimum grit removal for more than 30 years in the UK and USA. Headcell® is capable of achieving 95% removal of all grit 75 μm and larger. Because of its no-moving part design involving a hydraulically driven system, it delivers grit removal over a wide range of flows in a much smaller energy footprint than the conventional removal systems (Barter and Sherony, 2011) . chunks.text: Membrane aerated biofilm reactor (MABR), which can provide oxygen without forming bubbles, appears to be a potential solution. In MABR, oxygen is supplied through the gas-permeable membranes to avoid dCH 4 stripping, while other substrates (e.g., ammonium and dCH 4 ) come from the bulk liquid. The counter-diffusion of oxygen and other substrates present in wastewater creates a stratified biofilm system, where aerobic microorganisms theoretically occupy the inner layer of the biofilm while anaerobic microorganisms dominate in the outer layer. Consequently, integrating PN, anammox, and n-DAMO processes in MABR could be applied to simultaneously remove both dCH 4 and nitrogen. The present work aims to experimentally explore the feasibility of integrating PN, Anammox and Methane-dependent nitrite/nitrate reduction (PNAM) in an MABR system for the simultaneous removal of dCH 4 and nitrogen from anaerobically treated mainstream wastewater. To this end, a lab-scale MABR was established and operated for 350 days.

The combination of NF and RO membrane have also been demonstrated which resulted in significant improvement in the removal of COD and TDS with decrease in conductivity. Nataraj et al. [31] used membrane-based nanofiltration and reverse osmosis process combination for treatment of distillery wastewater which resulted in 99.8 % TDS reduction, 99.9 % COD reduction and 99.99 % potassium removal. The use of the membrane process is associated with serval drawbacks like fouling, flux decline, secondary waste generation and requirement of repetitive chemical cleaning especially for the streams having higher COD concentrations [32] . The membrane bioreactor (MBR) is one of the important process for treatment of sewage water. However, membrane fouling has been reported as one of the major drawback of MBR due to activated sludge liquor, biological flocs and soluble colloidal compounds.

chunks.text: In order to recover the lipid-rich biomass from the treated wastewaters and to further reduce the level of COD in the respective wastewaters, microfiltration using a low-cost ceramic membrane (pore size: 1.01 μm and porosity: 44%) was carried out. Fig. 6 presents the membrane flux and COD removal (%) from the different wastewaters at various operating pressures in the range of 34-172 kPa. With an increase in the operating pressure, the flux of the microfiltration system increased due to a high driving force acting on the membrane surface. The membrane flux was lower for DWW and PPWW as compared with that for the BGWW due to membrane fouling. In general, the membrane fouling is attributed to concentration polarization on the membrane surface and blocking of pores in the porous ceramic structure. In case of DWW and PPWW, fouling of the membrane was observed due to the adsorption of organic solutes/lignin and membrane surface polarization that creates further resistance to the transport of liquid through the membrane [1] . On the other hand, the less viscous BGWW possesses persistent organics [22] , and hence do not affect the membrane flux largely.

chunks.text: In the activated sludge process the majority of biological solids removed in the secondary sedimentation tank are recycled (returned sludge). The feedback of most of the cell yields from the sedimentation tank encourages rapid adsorption of the pollutants in the incoming settled sewage and also serves to stabilize the operation over a wide range of dilution rates and substrate concentrations imposed by fluctuations in the flow and strength of the wastewater. Secondary treatment processes can remove up to 95 per cent of the BOD and suspended solids entering the process, as well as significant amounts of heavy metals and certain organic compounds which could otherwise cause the deterioration of chemical and ecological quality of receiving waters [10, 53] . Conventional wastewater treatment usually ends with secondary treatment which cannot efficiently remove all the different compounds found in sewage and therefore treated effluents are one of the main sources of persistent micropollutants in the environment [1, 62] . For water reuse, tertiary treatment is needed to provide additional removal of contaminants such as microbial pathogens, particulates, or nutrients, and advanced treatment processes are employed when wastewater is to be reclaimed for reuse, depending on the type of use and quality requirements [49] .
